reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A chronic granulomatous dermatosis presenting as well-demarcated plaques with a yellow-brown, atrophic, waxy centre and a raised violaceous border
Most commonly affects the pretibial skin (shins), usually bilaterally, and is more frequent in women
Prominent telangiectasia and a shiny, atrophic surface through which underlying vessels are visible are characteristic
Classically associated with diabetes mellitus, though it occurs in non-diabetic individuals and its course does not track tightly with glycaemic control
Ulceration, often precipitated by minor trauma, is a common and troublesome complication
Histology shows layered ('palisaded') necrobiotic collagen degeneration with granulomatous inflammation throughout the dermis
Long-standing lesions carry a small risk of squamous cell carcinoma developing within them
reference.pathophysiology: Necrobiosis lipoidica is a granulomatous disorder characterised by degeneration ('necrobiosis') of dermal collagen with surrounding palisaded granulomatous inflammation. Microangiopathy with vessel-wall thickening and altered collagen, plus immune-complex-mediated vascular injury, are thought to compromise dermal blood supply and connective-tissue integrity, producing the atrophic, telangiectatic plaques. Although strongly linked with diabetes mellitus and its microvascular disease, the association is not absolute and glycaemic control does not reliably alter the skin lesions, indicating that additional immune and vascular mechanisms contribute.
additionalDifferentials: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma arising within a chronic plaque
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing palisaded necrobiotic granulomas (with caution given poor healing at biopsy sites)
Fasting glucose and HbA1c to screen for or monitor diabetes mellitus
Assessment for associated microvascular complications in diabetic patients
Wound assessment and swab if ulceration or secondary infection is suspected
Thyroid function and other autoimmune screening where clinically indicated
Biopsy of any non-healing or indurated area to exclude squamous cell carcinoma
redFlags: Chronic non-healing ulceration with signs of secondary infection
Nodular growth or induration within a long-standing plaque suggesting squamous cell carcinoma
Newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus uncovered during evaluation
Rapidly enlarging or atypical lesions requiring reassessment
reference.prognosis: Necrobiosis lipoidica is chronic and often persistent; lesions may slowly enlarge and can ulcerate, treatment responses are variable, and only a minority resolve spontaneously, with squamous cell carcinoma a rare long-term complication.
pitfalls: Assuming tight glycaemic control will clear the skin lesions
Biopsying pretibial lesions without anticipating poor wound healing and ulceration
Overlooking malignant transformation in a chronic non-healing plaque
Confusing it with granuloma annulare or stasis dermatitis and mismanaging accordingly
management: First-line potent topical or intralesional corticosteroids applied to the active raised border, with topical calcineurin inhibitors as an alternative
Systemic agents for refractory or ulcerating disease, such as tetracyclines, antimalarials, pentoxifylline or TNF-alpha inhibitors
Optimisation of glycaemic control and cardiovascular risk factors, while recognising the skin lesions may not track with glucose control
Meticulous wound care for ulceration, protection of the shins from trauma and compression for associated oedema
Smoking cessation to improve dermal microvascular perfusion
Surveillance biopsy of any non-healing or indurated lesion to exclude squamous cell carcinoma
Dermatology referral for diagnosis and management of resistant disease
